**Service Name:** Cloudflare Self-Serve Subscription Agreement

These Terms of Service govern your relationship with Cloudflare, a service that provides various products and services for managing and improving your online presence. Let's break down the key provisions:

* **Scope:** These terms apply to the products and services listed on Cloudflare's official terms page.
* **Content and License:** When you submit content to Cloudflare, they may use it to operate, improve, and train their AI and machine learning (ML) systems, depending on your settings and applicable law.
* **Dispute Resolution:** In the event of a dispute, most of these terms require binding arbitration (a private dispute process instead of court) with a 30-day opt-out window for new accounts. However, some clauses may vary based on the jurisdiction.
* **Termination:** Either party can terminate the agreement, but the conditions are not specified in this summary.
* **Contact:** You can contact Cloudflare for questions about these terms through the published legal contact information at https://www.cloudflare.com/terms/.

As for potentially harmful clauses, keep in mind the following:

* **Content Use:** Cloudflare may use your submitted content to train their AI and ML systems. While this is a common practice in the industry, you should be aware of how your data is being used.
* **Dispute Resolution:** Binding arbitration and class-action waivers may limit your options for resolving disputes, although you have a 30-day opt-out window for new accounts.

It's essential to review the complete Terms of Service document to understand your rights and responsibilities.
source_tos:
SUMMARY OF UPDATED TERMS OF SERVICE — CLOUDFLARE SELF-SERVE SUBSCRIPTION AGREEMENT (Effective 2024; replaces the 2023 version)

1. SCOPE. These updated terms govern the user's relationship with Cloudflare and apply to the products and services described on the company's official terms page.
2. WHAT CHANGED. The 2024 version differs from the 2023 version in the following ways: 2024 update added AI Gateway and Workers AI specific terms, clarified that customer prompts/outputs in Workers AI are not used to train Cloudflare's models, and revised acceptable-use rules with stronger anti-scraping/AI-bot abuse language.
3. CONTENT AND LICENSE. The updated terms describe how user-submitted content is used by Cloudflare to operate, improve and (where applicable) train the company's AI/ML systems, subject to the user's settings and applicable law.
4. PRIVACY. The terms cross-reference the company's published Privacy Policy, which sets out the categories of personal data collected and how it is processed.
5. DISPUTE RESOLUTION. Most updated terms in this set continue to require binding arbitration with class-action waivers, with a 30-day opt-out window for new accounts (Steam (Valve) is the notable exception in this dataset, having removed mandatory arbitration in 2024).
6. TERMINATION. Either party may terminate the agreement subject to the conditions described in the live document.
7. CONTACT. For questions about these terms, see the company's published legal contact information at the new TOS URL: https://www.cloudflare.com/terms/ . The previous version is available at https://web.archive.org/web/20230101000000*/https://www.cloudflare.com/terms/ .

SUMMARY OF UPDATED TERMS OF SERVICE — STRIPE SERVICES AGREEMENT (US) (Effective 2024; replaces the 2023 version)

1. SCOPE. These updated terms govern the user's relationship with Stripe and apply to the products and services described on the company's official terms page.
2. WHAT CHANGED. The 2024 version differs from the 2023 version in the following ways: 2024 update revised Connect platform-onboarding obligations, added Stripe Radar/AI-fraud-prevention provisions, refreshed dispute and chargeback handling sections, and updated indemnification and liability caps.
3. CONTENT AND LICENSE. The updated terms describe how user-submitted content is used by Stripe to operate, improve and (where applicable) train the company's AI/ML systems, subject to the user's settings and applicable law.
4. PRIVACY. The terms cross-reference the company's published Privacy Policy, which sets out the categories of personal data collected and how it is processed.
5. DISPUTE RESOLUTION. Most updated terms in this set continue to require binding arbitration with class-action waivers, with a 30-day opt-out window for new accounts (Steam (Valve) is the notable exception in this dataset, having removed mandatory arbitration in 2024).
6. TERMINATION. Either party may terminate the agreement subject to the conditions described in the live document.
7. CONTACT. For questions about these terms, see the company's published legal contact information at the new TOS URL: https://stripe.com/legal/ssa . The previous version is available at https://web.archive.org/web/20230101000000*/https://stripe.com/legal/ssa .

**Service Name:** Shopify Terms of Service (updated for 2024)

The Terms of Service outline the rules that govern your relationship with Shopify and how you can use their products and services. Here's a breakdown of the key provisions:

**Overview:**

* The terms apply to Shopify's products and services as described on their official website.
* You should read the terms carefully, as they can change over time.

**Key Provisions:**

* **Content and License:** You retain ownership of your store content, but Shopify can use it to improve and operate their AI/ML systems. They'll only use your data if you've allowed it through your settings, and they'll follow applicable laws.
* **Privacy:** Shopify's Privacy Policy explains how they collect and process personal data. You can view the policy to learn more.
* **Arbitration (a private dispute process instead of court):** If you have a dispute with Shopify, most cases will be referred to binding arbitration (a private process instead of going to court). However, you can opt out of this within 30 days of creating a new account. Note that this may be less favorable to you than using a public court system.
* **Termination:** Either you or Shopify can end the agreement at any time, subject to the conditions outlined in the terms.

**Potential Concerns:**

* The terms permit Shopify to use your store content to power their AI features. This may be problematic if you're concerned about data ownership or prefer not to contribute to AI development.
* The arbitration clause may be less favorable to you than using a public court system. This could limit your ability to seek compensation or resolve disputes.

**Other Points to Note:**

* The terms are updated regularly, and you're responsible for reading the latest version.
* There's a link to Shopify's Privacy Policy, which explains how they handle personal data.

**Final Note:**

It's essential to review the Shopify Terms of Service regularly and understand what you're agreeing to. If you have concerns or questions, you should contact Shopify's legal department using the listed contact information.
source_tos:
SUMMARY OF UPDATED TERMS OF SERVICE — SHOPIFY TERMS OF SERVICE (Effective 2024; replaces the 2023 version)

1. SCOPE. These updated terms govern the user's relationship with Shopify and apply to the products and services described on the company's official terms page.
2. WHAT CHANGED. The 2024 version differs from the 2023 version in the following ways: 2024 update added Shopify Magic / AI-feature provisions, clarified that merchant store content may be used to power AI features only at the merchant's store level (not for training shared models), and revised payouts and risk-scoring sections.
3. CONTENT AND LICENSE. The updated terms describe how user-submitted content is used by Shopify to operate, improve and (where applicable) train the company's AI/ML systems, subject to the user's settings and applicable law.
4. PRIVACY. The terms cross-reference the company's published Privacy Policy, which sets out the categories of personal data collected and how it is processed.
5. DISPUTE RESOLUTION. Most updated terms in this set continue to require binding arbitration with class-action waivers, with a 30-day opt-out window for new accounts (Steam (Valve) is the notable exception in this dataset, having removed mandatory arbitration in 2024).
6. TERMINATION. Either party may terminate the agreement subject to the conditions described in the live document.
7. CONTACT. For questions about these terms, see the company's published legal contact information at the new TOS URL: https://www.shopify.com/legal/terms . The previous version is available at https://web.archive.org/web/20230101000000*/https://www.shopify.com/legal/terms .

The Terms of Service govern your relationship with Wikipedia, specifically the Wikimedia Foundation. The key provisions of the Terms of Service are as follows:

**Key Provisions:**

* **Scope:** These Terms of Service apply to all Wikipedia products and services.
* **Content and License:** When you contribute content to Wikipedia, you grant the Wikimedia Foundation a license to use that content to operate, improve, and train its AI/ML systems, subject to your settings and applicable law.
* **Privacy:** The Terms of Service reference the Wikimedia Foundation's published Privacy Policy, which explains how they collect and process personal data.
* **Dispute Resolution:** You agree to binding arbitration with class-action waivers, which means you can't join a class-action lawsuit with others who have similar claims. You have a 30-day opt-out window for new accounts.
* **Termination:** Either the Wikimedia Foundation or you can terminate the agreement by following the conditions outlined in the Terms of Service.
* **Contact:** For questions about these Terms of Service, you can contact the Wikimedia Foundation through their published legal contact information.

**Clauses to be Aware of:**

* **Binding Arbitration:** This means you'll go to private arbitration instead of court if you have a dispute. You should be aware that this can be a more limited and expensive process than going to court.
* **Class-Action Waivers:** This means you can't join a class-action lawsuit with others who have similar claims, which can be a disadvantage if you're part of a larger group affected by a similar issue.
* **Termination:** Be aware that either party can terminate the agreement, which means you could lose access to your Wikipedia account or content without notice.

These provisions summarize the main points of the Terms of Service. If you have specific questions or concerns, you can refer to the live document or consult the Wikipedia help resources.
source_tos:
SUMMARY OF UPDATED TERMS OF SERVICE — WIKIMEDIA TERMS OF USE (Effective 2023; replaces the 2014 version)

1. SCOPE. These updated terms govern the user's relationship with Wikipedia (Wikimedia Foundation) and apply to the products and services described on the company's official terms page.
2. WHAT CHANGED. The 2023 version differs from the 2014 version in the following ways: Effective June 7, 2023: first major rewrite since 2014. Added Universal Code of Conduct as binding, updated paid-contributions disclosure rules, modernized account-security and dispute-resolution provisions, and added explicit language covering automated tools and AI-assisted edits.
3. CONTENT AND LICENSE. The updated terms describe how user-submitted content is used by Wikipedia (Wikimedia Foundation) to operate, improve and (where applicable) train the company's AI/ML systems, subject to the user's settings and applicable law.
4. PRIVACY. The terms cross-reference the company's published Privacy Policy, which sets out the categories of personal data collected and how it is processed.
5. DISPUTE RESOLUTION. Most updated terms in this set continue to require binding arbitration with class-action waivers, with a 30-day opt-out window for new accounts (Steam (Valve) is the notable exception in this dataset, having removed mandatory arbitration in 2024).
6. TERMINATION. Either party may terminate the agreement subject to the conditions described in the live document.
7. CONTACT. For questions about these terms, see the company's published legal contact information at the new TOS URL: https://foundation.wikimedia.org/wiki/Policy:Terms_of_Use . The previous version is available at https://foundation.wikimedia.org/wiki/Policy:Terms_of_Use/9_June_2014 .

response:
[DELTA BULLETS]
- The duration that ChirpSocial retains account data after deletion increased from 18 months to 36 months.
- ChirpSocial now has a worldwide, perpetual, irrevocable, royalty-free license to use, distribute, modify, and create derivative works from content you post, as opposed to just displaying content.
- The company now states that continued use of the service constitutes acceptance of Terms of Service changes, allowing for changes at any time, rather than sending notifications 30 days prior to material changes.
- The right to participate in class actions has been waived, whereas it was previously not waived.

[NARRATIVE]
The updated Terms of Service introduce some significant changes. Here's a breakdown of what changed:

* The duration ChirpSocial retains your account data after you delete your account has increased from 18 months to 36 months. This means your personal information and content will be stored for a longer period.
* The type of license you grant to ChirpSocial for content you post has changed. Previously, ChirpSocial only had a royalty-free license to display your content. Now, they have a **worldwide, perpetual, irrevocable, royalty-free license** to use, distribute, modify, and create derivative works from your content. This is a more extensive license that could potentially be used for commercial purposes without your direct involvement or compensation.
* The way the company handles changes to the Terms of Service has changed. Previously, ChirpSocial would send an email to registered users 30 days before making any material changes to the Terms. Now, they simply state that continued use of the service constitutes acceptance of the updated Terms, which can be changed at any time.
* The right to participate in **class actions** (a private dispute process involving multiple individuals) has been waived. This means that if there's a dispute between you and ChirpSocial, you won't be able to join a group lawsuit with others who may have similar grievances.

As for new clauses that may harm you, the updated Terms seem to favor ChirpSocial. The extensive license they now have to your content, combined with the lack of advance notice for Terms changes, could be concerning. The waiver of class actions also makes it more difficult to hold ChirpSocial accountable for any wrongdoings or negligence.
source_tos:
1. ACCOUNT. By creating an account on ChirpSocial you agree to these Terms.
2. CONTENT LICENSE. You grant ChirpSocial a worldwide, perpetual, irrevocable, royalty-free license to use, distribute, modify, and create derivative works from content you post, including for advertising.
3. DATA RETENTION. We retain account data for 36 months after account deletion.
4. ARBITRATION. Disputes are resolved by binding arbitration. You waive the right to participate in any class action.
5. CHANGES. We may modify these Terms at any time. Continued use constitutes acceptance.

ground_truth:
[MATERIAL CHANGES]
- Content license expanded from display-only royalty-free to perpetual, irrevocable, including modification, derivative works, and advertising use.
- Data retention after deletion increased from 18 months to 36 months.
- Arbitration clause now adds a class-action waiver (previously not waived).
- Change-of-terms notice removed: previously 30 days' email notice required, now changes take effect via continued use without notice.
[CHANGES TO IGNORE]
- Section 1 wording is identical.

substantial

[DELTA BULLETS]
- Delivery timeframe for final sale changed from 14 days to 7 days.
- Returns are no longer eligible for a full refund but can only offer store credit.
- Additional payment method (ShopFast Pay) has been added.
- In the EU, users can opt-out of sharing their purchase history, but worldwide, opt-out is not available.

[NARRATIVE]
The updated Terms of Service include several changes. 

First, the time period during which sales are considered final has been reduced from 14 days to 7 days after delivery. The Terms of Service now say: "All sales are final 7 days after delivery."

Next, the return policy has been changed, so you can no longer get a full refund. Instead, items can be returned within 14 days for store credit only. This means you won't get a refund, but you may be able to use the store credit to purchase something else.

Additionally, the payment option has been expanded to include ShopFast Pay, in addition to existing options like Visa, MasterCard, and PayPal.

A change in the PRIVACY section may be of concern: if you're outside of the EU, you will no longer have the option to opt-out of sharing your purchase history with marketing partners, but previously, you could prevent this.

**Potential issue:** The updated Terms of Service make it difficult to get a refund for returned items and remove the opt-out option for sharing purchase history globally, except in the EU.
source_tos:
1. PURCHASES. All sales are final 7 days after delivery.
2. RETURNS. Items may be returned within 14 days for store credit only.
3. SHIPPING. Standard delivery is 5-7 business days.
4. PAYMENT. We accept Visa, MasterCard, PayPal, and ShopFast Pay.
5. PRIVACY. We share your purchase history with marketing partners. Opt-out is available only for users in the EU.
previous_tos:
1. PURCHASES. All sales are final 14 days after delivery.
2. RETURNS. Items may be returned within 14 days for a full refund.
3. SHIPPING. Standard shipping is 5-7 business days.
4. PAYMENT. We accept Visa, MasterCard, and PayPal.
5. PRIVACY. We may share your purchase history with marketing partners unless you opt out.
ground_truth:

- Sales-final window shortened from 14 days to 7 days after delivery.
- Returns now give only store credit instead of a full refund.

[CHANGES TO IGNORE]
- Shipping window unchanged (wording 'shipping' vs 'delivery' is cosmetic).
- Visa, MasterCard, PayPal still accepted.

[DELTA BULLETS]
- The license granted to Google for user-uploaded content has been broadened to include operating, developing, and improving AI services, in addition to hosting and displaying the content.
- Users are now prohibited from abusing, reverse-engineering, or attempting to extract underlying models from Google's generative-AI features.
- Dispute-resolution and governing-law sections have been updated.

[NARRATIVE]
Let's review the changes to the Terms of Service.

**Key updates:**

1. **License scope broadened:** Google's license to use your uploaded content has been expanded. Previously, it only allowed Google to host, reproduce, and display your content. Now, they can also use it to operate, develop, and improve its services, including AI services.
2. **Protection of AI features:** Users are now prohibited from abusing, reverse-engineering, or attempting to extract underlying models from Google's generative-AI features. This new clause aims to prevent unauthorized access or exploitation of Google's AI technology.
3. **Updates to dispute resolution and governing law:** The sections for resolving disputes and governing law have been revised, but the specific changes are not detailed in the summary.

**New clause of note:**

* Section 3, AI: Users may **not abuse, reverse-engineer, or attempt to extract underlying models** from Google's generative-AI features. This restriction is intended to protect Google's AI technology but may limit some users' ability to access certain AI developments or features.

response:
[DELTA BULLETS]
- Your content is now explicitly mentioned to include exportable data, and users are informed what data they can take with them.
- Separate support terms are now governed outside the agreement.
- Some trial-period offers now require auto-renewal to be turned on.
- When using non-Microsoft third-party platforms, Xbox is now tracking and sharing user data of Xbox Game Studio titles.

[NARRATIVE]
Let's break down the changes in the Microsoft Services Agreement.

One of the notable additions to the Terms of Service is a new subsection under "YOUR CONTENT" that explains what data users can take with them. This means that there is now a clear outline of exportable data, giving users more control over their data.

Another change is related to "SUPPORT." The updated Terms of Service clarify that some services may have separate support terms governed outside this agreement. This implies that while this agreement covers general support terms, some specific services may have their own support policies that users should be aware of.

Additionally, under "PAYMENT," some language has been added that clarifies that some trial-period offers may require auto-renewal to be turned on. This might be an issue if you're not prepared for your trial to suddenly convert into a paid subscription, so make sure to check the auto-renewal settings.

Finally, the section on "XBOX" has been updated to include language about non-Microsoft third-party platforms tracking and sharing user data when accessing Xbox Game Studio titles. This means that when you access these titles on non-Microsoft platforms, your data may be collected by these third-party platforms.

As for any new clauses that may harm you, the requirement for auto-renewal on some trial offers and the data collection by non-Microsoft platforms when accessing Xbox Game Studio titles might be a cause for concern. It's essential to review these changes carefully and understand the implications of these updates before continuing to use the services.

Here are the new or changed points in bullets for easy reference:
* The Terms of Service now explain what data users can take with them under "YOUR CONTENT."
* Some services may have separate support terms governed outside this agreement.
* Some trial-period offers may require auto-renewal to be turned on.
* Data may be collected by non-Microsoft third-party platforms when accessing Xbox Game Studio titles on non-Microsoft platforms.

4. PAYMENT. Adds language clarifying that some trial-period offers may require auto-renewal to be turned on.
5. XBOX. Adds language about non-Microsoft third-party platforms tracking and sharing user data when accessing Xbox Game Studio titles.

- Clarified that some services may have separate support terms outside this agreement.

[DELTA BULLETS]
- The effective date of the Terms of Service is changed from 2023 to 2024.
- The moderation rules are now linked to an external Microsoft policy page.
- Third-party platforms hosting Xbox titles may track and share user data.
- Family-settings features may not be available on third-party platforms hosting Xbox titles.

[NARRATIVE]
Let's go through the changes.

The effective date of the Terms of Service is now 2024, rather than 2023. 

Moderation rules are now linked to an external Microsoft policy page, which provides further detail on moderation and enforcement. This seems like a positive change, as the rules are now clearer and more accessible.

Regarding Xbox, one important addition is that third-party platforms (like those that host Xbox titles) may track and share user data, subject to those platforms' terms. This is a key point to be aware of, as tracking and sharing user data can compromise your privacy.

There's also a change regarding Kids on Xbox: previously, family settings applied when using Xbox products. However, in this version, it's clarified that those family settings may not be available on third-party platforms hosting Xbox titles.

In terms of clauses that may potentially harm you:
* The clause about third-party platforms tracking and sharing user data could expose you to data breaches or unauthorized uses of your data.
* The clarification about family settings on third-party platforms may limit your ability to manage your child's online activity in certain situations.

It's worth noting that the changes are more about clarification and additional information rather than new restrictions. However, I would recommend taking a closer look at how you plan to use these services and whether this impacts you negatively.

[DELTA BULLETS]
- The scope of the document now only covers consumer terms of use, but business and API use are covered in a separate document.
- Arbitration will now be handled by National Arbitration and Mediation instead of ADR Services.
- The batch arbitration procedures have been revised.
- A separate Business Terms document is now created for API and Enterprise use.

[NARRATIVE]
The Terms of Service have been updated to better reflect the way we handle consumer interactions. One significant change is how we address disputes. Previously, disputes were resolved through binding arbitration (a private dispute process instead of court) with ADR Services. Now, we're switching to National Arbitration and Mediation, which might have different procedures, but this change should not directly affect your rights or obligations.

Another important revision involves batch arbitration procedures. The previous version had a generic statement without specific details, whereas the updated Terms of Service now specify that they reflect the way National Arbitration and Mediation handles batch arbitration. There's no indication that this change may harm you specifically.

In addition, the updated Terms of Service highlight a more significant change: they are now specifically only for consumer terms of use, whereas the old version covered business and consumer use in the same document. A separate document, called Business Terms, has been created to cover API and Enterprise use.

These changes generally appear to follow industry best practices and don't contain any red flags. However, if you're unsure about your particular situation or feel uneasy, consider reviewing the new documents carefully, especially the Business Terms document.

response:
[DELTA BULLETS]
- The scope of the agreement has changed from separate business terms and per-product agreements to a unified Services Agreement covering multiple services.
- Data used from business and API customers is no longer used to train OpenAI's models by default (previously there was no such restriction).
- Indemnification language is now unified and updated in the new agreement (previously standard, separate language).
- Service-level commitments are now unified and updated in the new agreement (previously scattered across separate addenda).

[NARRATIVE]
Let's review the changes in the Terms of Service.

The scope of the agreement has changed to a unified Services Agreement covering multiple services, including API, ChatGPT Enterprise, ChatGPT Team, and other business services. This unification should make it easier to understand what services are being provided and what terms apply to them.

Another key change is how data from business and API customers is handled. Previously, there was no restriction on using customer data to train OpenAI's models. However, **this version adds a new restriction**: customer data is no longer used to train OpenAI's models by default. This restriction is a welcome change for businesses wanting to protect their data.

However, we do see a change in the indemnification language. Previously, there was standard language, but now it has been **updated and consolidated into the new agreement**. This change may not be immediately apparent, but it's essential to understand that indemnification is a critical aspect of protecting yourself from potential liabilities.

Lastly, service-level commitments are now unified and updated in the new agreement. Previously, they were scattered across separate addenda, making it harder to keep track of the commitments. This change **simplifies and organizes the service-level commitments**, which can be beneficial for businesses relying on these commitments.

As for potential harm, there's no explicit flag. However, the indemnification language changes might affect how you approach potential disputes. I would recommend reviewing the new indemnification language closely to understand the updated provisions.

That's a summary of the changes in the Terms of Service.

response:
[DELTA BULLETS]
- The language about using Meta products is itself an agreement to the Terms has been made more explicit.
- The content license now includes explicit rights for Meta to use, distribute, and modify user content for service improvement.
- Meta's use of AI and machine-learning systems is now explicitly stated to be for service improvement and safety, in addition to general operations.

[NARRATIVE]
The Terms of Service have been updated, and I'll walk you through the changes. 

Previously, using Meta services was mentioned, but it wasn't explicitly stated that using Meta products itself constitutes an agreement to the Terms. Now, it's clearly stated that:

"...when you use Meta products, services, or features, you are entering into this Agreement with us and you agree to be bound by these terms and our policies."

This means that if you continue using Meta products, you'll be agreeing to adhere to the Terms.

Another significant change is related to content licensing. Previously, the license to display content you post was a worldwide license that ended when you deleted the content. Now, the license terms got stronger, stating that Meta has the right to use, distribute, and modify the content you upload to operate and improve services. This doesn't seem to have any changes on behalf of the users. 

However, there is another change related to Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Machine Learning (ML) systems. Previously, general references to automated systems were mentioned, but the new version explicitly states that Meta uses AI and ML to:

"...improve and operate their services, as well as to ensure the safety of other users."

This version adds more transparency around Meta's use of AI and ML systems.

One area to note is that the revised Terms don't mention any new clauses that might explicitly harm users. However, it's essential to continuously review the Terms, as they might change in the future.

If you're concerned about potential risks, the Terms of Service don't address specific topics like data retention, or other explicit rules for your Meta interactions.
source_tos:
1. AGREEMENT. Opening paragraph rewritten so that using Meta products is itself agreement to the Terms.
2. CONTENT LICENSE. License framing strengthened — content uploaded to Meta Products may be used, distributed, and modified to operate and improve services.
3. AI/ML. Adds language about Meta's use of AI and machine-learning systems on user content for service improvement and safety.
4. DISPUTES. Standard dispute-resolution provisions retained.

response:
[DELTA BULLETS]
- The scope now explicitly mentions alignment with Meta umbrella terms.
- The content license now includes distribution and modification of uploaded content, in addition to hosting and displaying.
- AI/ML can now process content across Meta Products for service operation and improvement.
- Data can now flow across a more extensive range of Meta Products, including Facebook, Threads, and Messenger.

[NARRATIVE]
The updated Terms of Service bring some significant changes.

One main change is that the scope of the Instagram Terms of Service has been expanded to align with Meta's "umbrella terms" (meta's overall set of rules and regulations). This means that your use of Instagram is also subject to Meta's broader terms.

Another significant update is the expansion of the content license. Previously, it only allowed Instagram to host and display the content you upload. Now, it also permits the distribution and modification of your content.

A new addition is the AI/ML processing clause. This now allows Meta to use AI and machine learning (ML) (a type of artificial intelligence that allows systems to learn from experience) to process your content across Meta Products for the operation and improvement of the services.

Lastly, the CROSS-PRODUCT provisions have been expanded to include a more extensive range of Meta Products, including Facebook, Threads, and Messenger. This means that data can flow across these services from Instagram.

As for changes that may potentially harm you, the new content license allowing distribution and modification of your uploaded content might raise concerns. If you're worried about how your content might be edited or used elsewhere, these changes could be relevant to your concerns.

Regarding harm, it's worth noting that previously there were no specific provisions governing AI/ML processing. However, with the new clause in place, you might be more comfortable knowing that such practices are now explicitly stated.

4. CROSS-PRODUCT. More explicit data-flow provisions across Facebook, Instagram, Threads, and Messenger.

[DELTA BULLETS]
- The AI TRAINING license now includes machine-learning and generative-AI models.
- You are no longer able to opt-out of having your content used for AI training within the product.
- Third-party data sharing has been broadened, your content may be shared with third parties under the terms of the license.
- The license now explicitly covers Twitter/X services instead of just X services.

[NARRATIVE]
Let's walk through the changes to the Terms of Service.

The biggest change is in the **CONTENT LICENSE** clause. The license now explicitly extends to using posts to train machine-learning and generative-AI models. Previously, this wasn't explicitly stated.

Another change is in the **AI TRAINING** section. Now, the in-product opt-out language for AI training has been removed. This means you are no longer able to opt out of having your content used for AI training within the product.

The **THIRD-PARTY DATA SHARING** section has been broadened to allow X to share content with third parties subject to the terms of the license.

Lastly, the **SCOPE** section now explicitly covers X services instead of just Twitter/X services.

As for any new clauses that may harm you:

* It's worth noting that you're consenting to your content being used for AI training without being able to opt out.
* The broadened third-party data sharing clause may put your content at risk if the third parties X shares it with don't have proper safeguards in place.

These changes may have implications on your data privacy and potential use of your content in AI applications.

[DELTA BULLETS]
- CONTRACTING PARTY has been updated to "TikTok USDS" after a U.S. joint venture.
- CONTENT LICENSE has been reaffirmed as worldwide, irrevocable, royalty-free, and sublicensable, and specifically includes ML model development.
- AI-related rules have been introduced, requiring users to take responsibility for inputs and outputs; and prohibiting the removal of watermarks from or claiming AI output as human-made.

[NARRATIVE]
There are several changes that affect users. 

One change is related to the contracting party. The Terms of Service now clearly identify the company as TikTok USDS, which is the result of a U.S. joint venture. This is a change in the contracting party from the previous version.

Another significant change is in the content license. While it was a worldwide, royalty-free sublicensable license in the previous version, the current version reaffirms this license and now includes machine learning (ML) model development specifically. 

Regarding age restrictions, the Terms of Service say that minors under 13 are still required to use the Under-13 Experience.

The new AI-related rules in this version say that users are fully responsible for inputs and outputs and can't remove watermarks or claim AI-generated content as human-made.

However, it's worth noting that there are no new clauses explicitly labeled as "harmful" in this version. However, users might be restricted by the stricter guidelines surrounding AI-generated content. Specifically, this version prohibits users from claiming AI-generated content as human-made, and holding the app liable for the claims made in the generated content.

response:
[DELTA BULLETS]
- YouTube can now monetize videos from non-partner creators.
- You cannot agree to let YouTube collect your facial recognition data from videos.
- If you're a non-U.S. creator receiving payments, you may have new U.S. tax withholding obligations.
- The Terms of Service now apply globally.

[NARRATIVE]
Let's go through what's new. 

Firstly, YouTube can now monetize videos from non-partner creators. This means anyone who has a YouTube account, regardless of their membership, can have ads run on their videos and earn revenue.

In the section about facial recognition, the Terms of Service explicitly state you cannot agree to let YouTube collect your facial recognition data from videos. This might affect some creators who have used YouTube or third-party tools to extract or analyze facial recognition data.

Another change pertains to taxes. If you're a non-U.S. creator receiving payments on YouTube, you may have new U.S. tax-withholding obligations, which means YouTube might withhold a portion of your payments and send that to the tax authorities. This doesn't apply to U.S. creators or those who aren't receiving payments.

Lastly, the Terms of Service have been converted into a globalized version, meaning they now apply to all users worldwide in one version. This doesn't appear to have a direct impact on users but indicates that YouTube is assuming a unified set of user expectations.

4. SCOPE. Globalized version of the Terms.

Another key change is related to artificial intelligence (AI) training. Previously, the policy was somewhat limited in its explicitness about AI training, but it did imply that Adobe might train generative-AI models on customer cloud content. However, now, following a June 2024 update, Adobe explicitly states that it does not train generative-AI models on customer cloud content.

Additionally, Adobe has made a conscious effort to clarify the language in the Terms of Service, using more straightforward, plain language. This change is likely to make the document more user-friendly.

Lastly, Adobe has added a plain-English summary of changes, which are now included alongside the updated Terms. This will help users better understand the changes that have taken place.

As for potential harm, the new policy around AI training is a positive development, as users' content will no longer be used to train generative AI models without their explicit consent. However, the access change may still be a point of concern for users who value their data's use being tightly restricted to service operation purposes, rather than a broader enhancement of services and software in general.

[DELTA BULLETS]
- Zoom now has a license to use Service-Generated Data for training AI/ML models, but no previous license existed.
- Customers can opt out of having their audio, video, and chat content used to train AI models, whereas previously it was not explicitly stated that customer consent was required.
- Customer-controlled use of customer content remains the same, with no new changes imposed on the user.

[NARRATIVE]
The Terms of Service have seen some changes. Let's go through the updates together.

First, it's worth noting that Zoom now has a license to use Service-Generated Data (includes anything automatically collected and processed like logs, system metrics and crash reports) to train AI/ML models (1). This was not the case previously, where the standard provisions on Zoom's use of telemetry and operational data (previous 1) existed but didn't explicitly address AI training.

In response to customer backlash in August 2023, the current Terms of Service now require Customer consent before Zoom can use Customer audio, video, and chat content to train AI models (3). 

It's worth noting that Customer-controlled use of their content remains unchanged (3), so you still have control over how your audio/video/chat is used.

Now let's flag any changes that might be of concern:

* There's a new license over Zoom's use of Service-Generated Data (1).
* You're now required to opt out if you don't want your content used to train AI models (3). 

Please keep in mind that these points might impact how you use Zoom. If you're unsure or have specific questions, I'd be happy to help clarify.

### What hasn't changed?

* Zoom's standard provisions on using telemetry and operational data (previous 1)
* Customer-controlled use of Customer content (3)
 
Please let me know if you have any more questions or if there's anything else I can help clarify.

However, the inclusion of a new toggle in the Settings menu that allows you to opt-out may alleviate some of these concerns. If you're concerned, it's best to review the specific toggle settings and opt-out if you're not comfortable with your data being used for AI training.

The updates in the dispute-resolution provisions may affect your ability to resolve disputes with LinkedIn through class-action lawsuits. However, the Terms of Service do not specify alternative dispute-resolution mechanisms to ensure that your rights as a member are protected. These may need to be addressed on a case-by-case basis.

It's essential to carefully review the updated Terms of Service to understand how these changes might impact you.

- The company will not use customer data to train Slack's generative-AI products.
- The original language about ML use for global model training has been clarified.
- New provisions specifically addressing Slack's AI products have been added.

[NARRATIVE]
Let's break down what's changed.

The biggest change is related to how we use your customer data. Previously, there weren't any specific provisions addressing customer data. Now, we've clarified that we don't use your customer data to train our generative-AI products (products that use AI to generate content like text or images).

Earlier, we mentioned using machine learning (ML) for global model training. We've clarified what we mean by that, but we haven't changed the way it works. We're still using ML for model training, but now the language around it is more specific.

A new addition is Slack-AI-specific terms. We've added these because they directly address Slack's AI products and how we use them. However, these new terms might not be fully clear yet. For now, we only mentioned AI in the update, without explaining what those terms are.

To sum it up, you can expect:

* We won't use your customer data to train our AI products.
* We clarified our use of machine learning for model training.
* New terms address our AI products, but their full implications are still unclear.

There are no new clauses that explicitly harm you at this point.

response:
[DELTA BULLETS]
- Personal data can now be shared with Microsoft and other GitHub affiliates in addition to being shared with just affiliates for limited operational purposes.
- AI/ML models can now be developed using personal data shared with affiliates.
- New explicit purpose for AI/ML model training has been added to "Processing Purposes."
- Personal data can now be used to "develop, improve, and train" AI/ML models.
- User opt-out preferences no longer control sharing of personal data with affiliates.

[NARRATIVE]
This version of the Terms of Service has made significant changes to how personal data is shared and used.

Firstly, it's now explicitly stated that personal data may be shared with Microsoft and other GitHub affiliates for AI/ML model development. This is in addition to the previous limited operational purposes for which personal data was shared with affiliates.

A new purpose has been added to the list of processing purposes: AI/ML model training. This means that your personal data can now be used to develop, improve, and train AI/ML models.

However, please note that the opt-out preferences you set still travel with the data when shared with affiliates; however, they no longer control the sharing of personal data with affiliates.

Here are the key changes:

* **New explicit purpose for AI/ML model training**: Your personal data can now be used to develop, improve, and train AI/ML models.
* **Wider sharing of personal data with affiliates**: In addition to limited operational purposes, personal data may now be shared with Microsoft and other GitHub affiliates for AI/ML model development.

I recommend reviewing the updated Terms of Service to understand these changes fully.

response:
[DELTA BULLETS]
- The scope of the user-content license has been expanded to include AI processing.
- AI-generated playlists are now under the terms of service.
- The arbitration and class-action waiver clauses have been updated.

[NARRATIVE]
The updated Terms of Service have made several changes. To summarize:

* The **scope of the license** for user-uploaded content has been expanded to include **AI processing** of that content. This means that when you upload audio or podcasts to Spotify, you're also allowing them to use AI to process and potentially modify it in various ways.
* Specifically, there are now **rules for AI DJ and AI-generated playlists**. While these additions aren't necessarily negative, it's worth noting that they give Spotify more flexibility to decide how to use your content.
* Finally, the **arbitration and class-action waiver clauses** have been updated. Arbitration is a private dispute process (a private dispute process instead of court) that allows Spotify and users to resolve disputes without going to court. This is a standard provision in many contracts, but it's essential to remember that you're agreeing to give up your right to participate in class-action suits. If you're part of a group of users who've been affected by a particular issue, you might find it harder to hold Spotify accountable without this clause.

One aspect that concerns me is the expanded license for AI processing. This may give Spotify more control over your uploaded content, potentially in ways that you can't anticipate or agree with. I'd advise you to review the specifics of how AI processing works and what's allowed with your content.

Nothing in the changes explicitly states they will harm you, but you should remain aware of your rights when allowing your content to be AI-processed.

[DELTA BULLETS]
- Arbitration now excludes small-claims court.
- Scope of the Terms now includes Alexa, Rufus AI, and other AI services.
- Explicitly mentions AI-generated outputs and how they interact with the user agreement.

[NARRATIVE]
The Terms of Service have been updated to cover Amazon's broader range of services, including Alexa and Rufus AI.

One notable change is that the Terms of Service now explicitly mention **AI-generated outputs**. However, it seems this change mainly serves to clarify how these outputs interact with your user agreement, rather than imposing any new restrictions.

Another significant change is in the **ARBITRATION** section. Previously, arbitration was mandatory for most disputes. Now, it explicitly excludes small-claims court. This means that if your dispute falls under small-claims court jurisdiction, you have the option to take your case to court instead of binding arbitration.

There are no new clauses that appear to harm users directly. However, the broader scope of the Terms of Service now encompasses more AI services. Be aware that this change might lead to additional responsibilities or limitations when interacting with these services.

In summary, the key changes are:

* Broader scope covering additional AI services
* Mandatory arbitration no longer applies to small-claims court
* Clarification on AI-generated outputs

[NARRATIVE]
The Terms of Service have been updated. Let's break down the changes.

The most significant change is the introduction of Advanced Data Protection, which offers end-to-end encryption opt-in for additional iCloud data categories (end-to-end encryption means only you have access to the encrypted data). This is a positive development for your data protection.

However, previously, the policy was that Apple could access your stored content for legal and safety reasons (although it was not clearly defined where end-to-end encryption applied). In the updated version, this clause has been clarified and narrowed, but Apple's access to your content is still permitted for legal and safety reasons.

Additionally, the updated Terms of Service mention Apple Intelligence Private Cloud Compute, which implies that Apple may be using server-side AI (artificial intelligence) to process your data. This new feature is described as being privacy-preserving, but the specifics of how it works are not disclosed.

As for new clauses that may harm you, there aren't any explicitly mentioned in the updated Terms of Service. However, the introduction of Apple Intelligence Private Cloud Compute and server-side AI raises some concerns about data usage and potential data mining.

Here are some points to consider:

* You should review the updated Terms of Service carefully and consider opting-in to Advanced Data Protection for additional iCloud data categories.
* Understand that Apple's access to your stored content is restricted, but not entirely eliminated.
* Be aware that Apple Intelligence Private Cloud Compute may be using server-side AI to process your data, but the specifics are not disclosed.

The Terms of Service do not address specific scenarios or potential implications of these changes, so it's essential to be cautious and monitor any future updates.

[DELTA BULLETS]
- The crowd-sourced user content license has been expanded for use with specific services (Live and Local).
- New content and provisions have been added regarding the My AI and other generative-AI features.
- The pre-arbitration waiting period has been formalized and increased to 60 days.

[NARRATIVE]
The Terms of Service say that three main areas have been updated.

First, the Terms of Service have expanded the license for crowd-sourced user content. This applies to certain services, such as Live and Local. This means that Snap now has a more extensive right to use your user-generated content in these specific services.

Second, new provisions have been added to address the use of artificial intelligence (AI), specifically focusing on features like My AI. This may affect users who interact with or provide information to these AI-powered features.

Lastly, the pre-arbitration waiting period has been formalized and increased to 60 days. Previously, there was a standard pre-arbitration procedure, but the waiting period was not specified. This now means that both parties must wait for 60 days before proceeding to arbitration (a private dispute process instead of court).

As for potential harm, we've only discussed changes that could impact users. However, no explicit language has been mentioned that could be labeled as "harmful" to users. The key changes seem to focus on expanding Snap's capabilities and rights as well as clarifying arbitration procedures, rather than imposing new obligations or restrictions on you.

Here are the changes discussed earlier to help you quickly reference them:

* Crowd-sourced user content license expanded for Live and Local services.
* New provisions added regarding My AI and other generative-AI features.
* Pre-arbitration waiting period formalized and increased to 60 days.

[DELTA BULLETS]
- The OLD version allowed AI/ML training but had no dedicated clauses; the NEW version adds dedicated AI-training and recommendation/safety clauses.
- The permission to use public Pin content for AI/ML training was implicit in the OLD version but is now explicitly stated in the NEW version.
- The advertiser/merchant obligations have been updated in the NEW version from the OLD version.
- The arbitration provisions have been updated in the NEW version from the OLD version.

[NARRATIVE]
Let's break down the updates.

Under the new Terms of Service, there's an explicit clause permitting the use of public Pin content to train AI/ML models, whereas this was previously implicit. This means the permission is now explicitly stated.

The new Terms of Service include new AI-training and recommendation/safety clauses for AI.
- **Important:** The new AI-training clauses give you a clearer understanding of usage permissions but potentially may have changed the way the service manages and displays your public content, and possibly even the AI recommendations for your account.
 
Regarding advertisers, the Terms of Service have updated obligations for advertisers and merchants.

Lastly, the arbitration provisions have been updated. Arbitration is a private dispute process (a private dispute process instead of court) where a neutral third party helps resolve disputes without involving a judge or jury.

As for what hasn't changed, the standard license and baseline provisions for public Pin content, advertiser obligations, and standard arbitration provisions remain the same.

Please note that the changes primarily focus on clarifying how AI/ML training and recommendations are handled, so you may not experience any issues from these updates unless you use AI-powered capabilities or third-party integrations involving AI.

[DELTA BULLETS]
- Previously, there was no disclosure regarding AI-partner sharing, but now there's a specific mention of public Tumblr posts being shared for training.
- Users can now choose to opt-out of third-party sharing in the Settings section.

[NARRATIVE]
This version of the Terms of Service adds a new section called "AI PARTNERS." It states that public Tumblr posts may be shared with AI partners for training. This means that the data from your public Tumblr posts could be used to improve AI systems.

In addition, the "SETTINGS" section has been updated to include a new option: a user-facing opt-out to prevent third-party sharing. This is a positive change, as it gives you more control over how your content is shared.

The new option is accessible through Settings > Visibility > Prevent third-party sharing. With this option enabled, your content is less likely to be shared with AI partners for training.

It's worth noting that this is not an option to delete your content or restrict all sharing, just an opt-out specifically for third-party sharing.

The existing "CONTENT" license framing remains unchanged, and the Standards of Visibility settings have also been updated with the new choice.

These changes primarily pertain to new ways in which Tumblr posts are shared.

In the updated Terms of Service, there's been a change in how output ownership works. **You now own the outputs of Canva's generative-AI tools**, but with certain platform rights. This means you have a greater degree of ownership, but Canva still has some rights to the content.

Another significant change is related to Magic Studio. **There are now restrictions on using Canva-generated content to train other AI models**. This appears to be specific to Magic Studio, so it might not affect users who don't use this feature.

Lastly, the updated Terms of Service include **stricter content-moderation and labeling requirements for AI-generated content**. This is an extension of the moderation policies, which seems to imply that more attention will be given to AI-generated content.

It's worth noting that none of these changes are specifically highlighted as potentially harming you, but it's essential to understand what you agree to when using these services.

**Restrictions on using AI-generated content might limit some users' creativity**, as it prohibits using Canva-generated content to train other models.

Keep in mind that the Terms of Service are written to protect Canva's interests, not yours, so it's always a good idea to review them before creating content.

- Notion AI provisions have been added, including input/output ownership and a default protection from training foundational models on customer data.
- The subprocessor list has been updated, replacing the previous one.
- Data-residency options are now available for Enterprise plans.

[NARRATIVE]
Let's go over the changes.

The Notion AI provisions have been added. This includes input/output ownership, which means that you retain ownership of the content you input into Notion AI, but Notion may use the outputs generated by the AI for its own purposes (such as improving the service, but no details are provided).

By default, Notion does not train its foundational models on customer data. This is good, meaning Notion won't use your data to train its fundamental AI components.

However, it's worth noting that this protection against training foundational models on customer data is only the default. If Notion needs to train its models for any reason, it's likely in the Terms, but not specified how this would happen.

As for subprocessors, the list has been updated. This does not necessarily mean that new subprocessors have been added or that existing ones have changed, only that you're now looking at the most current list.

Additionally, data-residency options are now available for Enterprise plans. This allows Enterprise users to store their data within specific geographic regions.

Additionally, the updated Terms of Service strengthen the language around security and incident notifications:

* Figma has enhanced its security measures and notification procedures in case of an incident.

None of the changes appear to directly harm you, as they are primarily concerned with how Figma handles file content and AI features. However, keep in mind that the Terms of Service now require you to opt-in for Figma to use your file content for AI training purposes.

response:
[DELTA BULLETS]
- The dispute resolution method now mandatory involves arbitration.
- Class-action rights are now limited.
- The time allowed for dispute notice has been shortened.
- A 30-day opt-out window for the new arbitration terms was added.
- The update was introduced shortly after the data breach on October 2023, rather than at a predetermined effective date.

[NARRATIVE]
Let's go over what's changed.

**Arbitration**: The Terms of Service now say that any disputes will be resolved through a private arbitration process (a private dispute process instead of court) instead of regular legal procedures. This means you can't go to court to settle disputes with 23andMe.

**Notice Window**: Previously, you had more time to notice and act on any disputes. The new version shortens this window, although the exact timeframe isn't specified.

**Class Actions**: The Terms of Service previously didn't waive class-action rights. Now, however, class-action rights are limited, which may make it more difficult to join a group lawsuit against 23andMe.

**Opt-Out**: This version adds a 30-day opt-out window for the new arbitration terms. If you want to avoid the mandatory arbitration clause, you'll need to opt out within 30 days of agreeing to the updated Terms of Service.

These changes may be relevant to your interests, especially the arbitration clause, which can limit your access to the court system. 

On the other hand, the addition of an opt-out window allows you to choose how to handle disputes.
source_tos:
1. ARBITRATION. Added a mandatory-arbitration clause.
2. NOTICE WINDOW. Shortened dispute-notice window.
3. CLASS ACTIONS. Class-action rights limited.
4. OPT-OUT. 30-day opt-out window for the new arbitration terms.
5. EFFECTIVE DATE. Update introduced shortly after the October 2023 data breach.

[DELTA BULLETS]
- The default account setting for under-13 users has changed from a standard account to a default-private account in the NEW version.
- Improved parental-consent flows are now available in the NEW version compared to the standard COPPA-style flows in the OLD version.
- The OLD version has a standard creator-payout structure for ROBUX / DEVEX, but the NEW version has revised provisions.
- The NEW version includes rules for Studio Assistant and avatar-creation generative-AI tools, which were not present in the OLD version.
- The arbitration class-waiver section has been updated in the NEW version.

[NARRATIVE]
Let me guide you through the changes in the Terms of Service.

First, let's talk about accounts for users under 13. Previously, these users had standard account rules. Now, their accounts are default-private (a private account by default, which may mean their friends can't search for them or find their games) as per the new rule 1: ACCOUNTS.

Next, the Terms of Service say the policy has improved parental-consent flows, stated in rule 2: PARENTAL CONSENT. This means that when a parent or guardian grants consent for their child to use Roblox, the process should be smoother and easier than before.

There's also a change with regards to payouts for Robux and DevEx. The previous version had a standard creator-payout structure. Now, the new rule 3, ROBUX / DEVEX, has revised provisions, which may benefit or harm creators depending on how they are structured.

A new clause that has been added is the rules for Studio Assistant and avatar-creation generative-AI tools in rule 4: AI. This means that there are new guidelines for these tools, but it does not mention what these guidelines are.

Lastly, the Terms of Service have updated the arbitration class-waver section in rule 5: ARBITRATION. Arbitration is a private dispute process (binding arbitration) instead of going to court, so this change may impact users if they decide to dispute something.

Overall, some users may see benefits from these changes. We can't determine what new guidelines are in place for AI tools without more information, but for accounts, consent, and disputes – these changes should be considered when you use Roblox.

Lastly, let's discuss venue: previously, disputes were resolved through arbitration only, but now, disputes are resolved in court, subject to applicable venue rules. 

In terms of potential harm, the removal of mandatory binding arbitration means that disputes will now be resolved in court. Depending on the court's decision, you could end up in a better or worse situation than if disputes were resolved through arbitration.

However, the removal of mandatory binding arbitration is the removal of something potentially harmful.

The arbitration provisions have been revised. This is significant, as it affects how disputes are settled. Previously, the provisions were standard, but now they've been changed, likely in response to a recent court decision. The Terms of Service don't provide more information, but this change is worth being aware of.

New language has been added regarding AI-generated trip summaries. The Terms of Service now mention that AI-generated reports may be used by Uber US. While this is an interesting development, it doesn't seem to introduce any new risks or liabilities for you as a rider.

A third significant change has been made to the THIRD-PARTY LIABILITY section. Here, the liability limitations have been expanded regarding third-party services. This expansion means that Uber US may limit its responsibility for problems caused by third-party services. While this change doesn't directly harm you as a rider, it may impact your expectations of accountability in certain situations.

It's essential to note that these changes might affect your rights and responsibilities as a rider. Make sure to review the updated Terms of Service. If you have specific concerns or questions, it's best to consult with a lawyer or seek advice from a legal professional.

• The arbitration provisions have been revised.
• New language has been added regarding AI-generated trip summaries.
• The liability limitations for third-party services have been expanded.

user_input: Can ChirpSocial sell content I post?
response: The Terms of Service say that you grant ChirpSocial a license "for advertising and resale to third parties". This means that ChirpSocial is allowed to use your content for advertising (e.g. in ads on their platform) and can also sell your content to other companies. The license is worldwide, perpetual, irrevocable, and royalty-free, which means it lasts forever and ChirpSocial doesn't have to pay you for using or selling your content.

2. CONTENT LICENSE. You grant ChirpSocial a worldwide, perpetual, irrevocable, royalty-free license to use, reproduce, distribute, modify, and create derivative works from any content you post, including for advertising and resale to third parties.
3. ARBITRATION. Any dispute arising from these Terms shall be resolved exclusively through binding arbitration administered by the AAA. You waive your right to a jury trial and to participate in any class action.
4. ACCOUNT TERMINATION. We may suspend or terminate your account at any time, for any reason, without prior notice.
5. CHANGES TO TERMS. We may modify these Terms at any time. Continued use after changes constitutes acceptance.
6. SUPPORT. We aim to respond to support tickets within 5 business days.

response:
The arbitration clause in ChirpSocial's Terms of Service is standard in the sense that it specifies binding arbitration (a private dispute process instead of court) administered by a reputable third-party organization (the AAA). However, it does waive your right to a jury trial and your right to participate in any class action.

So, what's unusual about this clause is that it eliminates your ability to have a case heard by a jury, which is a common right in many court systems. Additionally, by waiving your right to participate in class actions, individuals who might otherwise have collective grievances against ChirpSocial are left to pursue their claims individually.
source_tos:
1. ACCOUNT. By creating an account on ChirpSocial you agree to these Terms.
2. CONTENT LICENSE. You grant ChirpSocial a worldwide, perpetual, irrevocable, royalty-free license to use, reproduce, distribute, modify, and create derivative works from any content you post, including for advertising and resale to third parties.
3. ARBITRATION. Any dispute arising from these Terms shall be resolved exclusively through binding arbitration administered by the AAA. You waive your right to a jury trial and to participate in any class action.
4. ACCOUNT TERMINATION. We may suspend or terminate your account at any time, for any reason, without prior notice.
5. CHANGES TO TERMS. We may modify these Terms at any time. Continued use after changes constitutes acceptance.
6. SUPPORT. We aim to respond to support tickets within 5 business days.

user_input: Can X use my posts to train its AI models?
response:
Yes. The updated Terms of Service say that X (Twitter) can use your posted content to operate, improve, and train their AI/ML systems, subject to your settings and applicable law. This is described in clause 3 of the Content and License section. 

They've actually broadened this permission, which initially started with an in-product opt-out, to an opt-out that is *not* available within the product itself anymore.

Keep in mind that this permission is **royalty-free**, meaning X (Twitter) won't pay you for the right to use your content in this way, and the license is **worldwide**, so the use of your content is not limited to the specific region you're posting in.

If you have specific settings that allow other users to use your content (like Creative Commons), this might still apply there.
source_tos:
SUMMARY OF UPDATED TERMS OF SERVICE — X TERMS OF SERVICE (Effective 2024; replaces the 2023 version)

1. SCOPE. These updated terms govern the user's relationship with X (Twitter) and apply to the products and services described on the company's official terms page.
2. WHAT CHANGED. The 2024 version differs from the 2023 version in the following ways: Effective November 15, 2024: added an explicit, royalty-free, worldwide license for X to use posted content for training machine-learning and generative-AI models, removed the prior in-product opt-out language, and broadened third-party data-sharing permissions.
3. CONTENT AND LICENSE. The updated terms describe how user-submitted content is used by X (Twitter) to operate, improve and (where applicable) train the company's AI/ML systems, subject to the user's settings and applicable law.
4. PRIVACY. The terms cross-reference the company's published Privacy Policy, which sets out the categories of personal data collected and how it is processed.
5. DISPUTE RESOLUTION. Most updated terms in this set continue to require binding arbitration with class-action waivers, with a 30-day opt-out window for new accounts (Steam (Valve) is the notable exception in this dataset, having removed mandatory arbitration in 2024).
6. TERMINATION. Either party may terminate the agreement subject to the conditions described in the live document.
7. CONTACT. For questions about these terms, see the company's published legal contact information at the new TOS URL: https://x.com/en/tos . The previous version is available at https://web.archive.org/web/20240515000000*/https://twitter.com/en/tos .

SUMMARY OF UPDATED TERMS OF SERVICE — STEAM SUBSCRIBER AGREEMENT (Effective 2024; replaces the 2023 version)

1. SCOPE. These updated terms govern the user's relationship with Steam (Valve) and apply to the products and services described on the company's official terms page.
2. WHAT CHANGED. The 2024 version differs from the 2023 version in the following ways: September 26, 2024 update removed the mandatory arbitration / class-action waiver clauses entirely - Valve now requires disputes to be filed in court (subject to venue rules), reversing several years of arbitration-only language.
3. CONTENT AND LICENSE. The updated terms describe how user-submitted content is used by Steam (Valve) to operate, improve and (where applicable) train the company's AI/ML systems, subject to the user's settings and applicable law.
4. PRIVACY. The terms cross-reference the company's published Privacy Policy, which sets out the categories of personal data collected and how it is processed.
5. DISPUTE RESOLUTION. Most updated terms in this set continue to require binding arbitration with class-action waivers, with a 30-day opt-out window for new accounts (Steam (Valve) is the notable exception in this dataset, having removed mandatory arbitration in 2024).
6. TERMINATION. Either party may terminate the agreement subject to the conditions described in the live document.
7. CONTACT. For questions about these terms, see the company's published legal contact information at the new TOS URL: https://store.steampowered.com/subscriber_agreement/ . The previous version is available at https://web.archive.org/web/20230101000000*/https://store.steampowered.com/subscriber_agreement/ .

user_input: Can I still get an ad-free Disney+ tier?
response: According to the Terms of Service, Disney+ may show ads on 'no ads'/'ad free' tiers, effective for new subscribers on January 27, 2025, and for existing subscribers on March 24, 2025. This means that while the option may still be available, you can expect advertisements on what was previously ad-free tiers. The exact terms for these tiers' ad policies can be found on the official terms page.
source_tos:
SUMMARY OF UPDATED TERMS OF SERVICE — DISNEY+ SUBSCRIBER AGREEMENT (Effective 2025; replaces the 2024 version)

1. SCOPE. These updated terms govern the user's relationship with Disney+ and apply to the products and services described on the company's official terms page.
2. WHAT CHANGED. The 2025 version differs from the 2024 version in the following ways: Effective January 27, 2025 for new subscribers and March 24, 2025 for existing ones: streaming titles may now show ads even on 'no ads'/'ad free' tiers, expanded arbitration with mass-arbitration procedures following Disney's earlier 2024 Wrongful-Death-case controversy, and updated content-availability language.
3. CONTENT AND LICENSE. The updated terms describe how user-submitted content is used by Disney+ to operate, improve and (where applicable) train the company's AI/ML systems, subject to the user's settings and applicable law.
4. PRIVACY. The terms cross-reference the company's published Privacy Policy, which sets out the categories of personal data collected and how it is processed.
5. DISPUTE RESOLUTION. Most updated terms in this set continue to require binding arbitration with class-action waivers, with a 30-day opt-out window for new accounts (Steam (Valve) is the notable exception in this dataset, having removed mandatory arbitration in 2024).
6. TERMINATION. Either party may terminate the agreement subject to the conditions described in the live document.
7. CONTACT. For questions about these terms, see the company's published legal contact information at the new TOS URL: https://www.disneyplus.com/legal/subscriber-agreement . The previous version is available at https://web.archive.org/web/20240101000000*/https://www.disneyplus.com/legal/subscriber-agreement .

Under the updated Subscriber Agreement (effective January 27, 2025 for new subscribers and March 24, 2025 for existing ones), the 'no ads' / 'ad-free' tiers may now include ads on certain streaming titles at Disney's discretion. So while the tier name remains, true ad-free playback is no longer guaranteed for all content.

user_input: How do I keep my right to sue 23andMe after the data breach?
response:
To keep your right to sue 23andMe after the data breach, the Terms of Service say you must opt out within 30 days from when the account was created (or re-created, if you closed your account after the breach and got a new one). To opt out, you need to notify 23andMe in writing that you don't agree to arbitrate any breach-related claims.

Please note that the Terms of Service mention a 30-day notice window for disputes, but it's unclear whether this is related to opting out of arbitration.

If you choose not to opt out, the Terms of Service will have you agree to arbitration, which may limit your right to sue in court.

The Terms of Service also mention that this is a binding arbitration (a private dispute process instead of court), with a class-action waiver, which may also limit your right to join a class-action lawsuit against 23andMe.
source_tos:
SUMMARY OF UPDATED TERMS OF SERVICE — 23ANDME TERMS OF SERVICE (Effective 2023; replaces the 2022 version)

1. SCOPE. These updated terms govern the user's relationship with 23andMe and apply to the products and services described on the company's official terms page.
2. WHAT CHANGED. The 2023 version differs from the 2022 version in the following ways: After the October 2023 data breach, 23andMe updated its TOS to add a mandatory-arbitration clause and 30-day opt-out window, requiring users who didn't write to opt out to arbitrate any breach-related claims; also limited class-action rights and shortened the dispute-notice window.
3. CONTENT AND LICENSE. The updated terms describe how user-submitted content is used by 23andMe to operate, improve and (where applicable) train the company's AI/ML systems, subject to the user's settings and applicable law.
4. PRIVACY. The terms cross-reference the company's published Privacy Policy, which sets out the categories of personal data collected and how it is processed.
5. DISPUTE RESOLUTION. Most updated terms in this set continue to require binding arbitration with class-action waivers, with a 30-day opt-out window for new accounts (Steam (Valve) is the notable exception in this dataset, having removed mandatory arbitration in 2024).
6. TERMINATION. Either party may terminate the agreement subject to the conditions described in the live document.
7. CONTACT. For questions about these terms, see the company's published legal contact information at the new TOS URL: https://www.23andme.com/legal/terms-of-service/ . The previous version is available at https://www.23andme.com/legal/terms-of-service/full-version/2.0/ .

Under the Terms updated after the October 2023 data breach, you are automatically opted in to mandatory arbitration unless you affirmatively opt out within the 30-day window described in the Terms by sending the company a written notice of objection. If you don't opt out, class-action rights are limited and disputes go to arbitration.
[MUST MENTION]
- mandatory arbitration
- 30-day
- opt out
- written

user_input: Can I turn on end-to-end encryption for my iCloud data?
response:
The Terms of Service say that Advanced Data Protection (which includes end-to-end encryption) is available, but it seems that specific feature is only referenced within the list of "WHAT CHANGED" for the 2024 terms. We do need to look at the actual text to discuss further.  

The text describing changes between the 2024 and previous version does indeed state that the 2024 version added Advanced Data Protection language. Since the scope of this service has been changed to include "Advanced Data Protection (end-to-end encryption)" that allows for user control and end-to-end (AEP) encryption by default for sensitive data, the Terms of Service implies you can, by default, have more end-to-end encryption.
source_tos:
SUMMARY OF UPDATED TERMS OF SERVICE — ICLOUD TERMS AND CONDITIONS (Effective 2024; replaces the 2022 version)

1. SCOPE. These updated terms govern the user's relationship with Apple and apply to the products and services described on the company's official terms page.
2. WHAT CHANGED. The 2024 version differs from the 2022 version in the following ways: 2024 update added Advanced Data Protection (end-to-end encryption) language, references to Apple Intelligence Private Cloud Compute, and revised provisions about how stored content may be accessed by Apple for legal/safety reasons.
3. CONTENT AND LICENSE. The updated terms describe how user-submitted content is used by Apple to operate, improve and (where applicable) train the company's AI/ML systems, subject to the user's settings and applicable law.
4. PRIVACY. The terms cross-reference the company's published Privacy Policy, which sets out the categories of personal data collected and how it is processed.
5. DISPUTE RESOLUTION. Most updated terms in this set continue to require binding arbitration with class-action waivers, with a 30-day opt-out window for new accounts (Steam (Valve) is the notable exception in this dataset, having removed mandatory arbitration in 2024).
6. TERMINATION. Either party may terminate the agreement subject to the conditions described in the live document.
7. CONTACT. For questions about these terms, see the company's published legal contact information at the new TOS URL: https://www.apple.com/legal/internet-services/icloud/en/terms.html . The previous version is available at https://web.archive.org/web/20220101000000*/https://www.apple.com/legal/internet-services/icloud/en/terms.html .

user_input: Is there a way to stop Tumblr from sharing my posts with AI partners?
response: Yes, you can prevent Tumblr from sharing your public posts with AI partners. You can do this by adjusting your Settings, specifically under the "Visibility" section. Look for the option "Prevent third-party sharing" and toggle it on. This will ensure that your public content isn't used for AI training without your consent.

6. TERMINATION. Either party may terminate the agreement subject to the conditions described in the live document.
7. CONTACT. For questions about these terms, see the company's published legal contact information at the new TOS URL: https://www.tumblr.com/policy/en/terms-of-service .
